claim: Both endogenous antibodies and a subset of antibody therapeutics engage Fc gamma receptor (FcγR)IIIa/CD16a to stimulate a protective immune response.
source: Both endogenous antibodies and a subset of antibody therapeutics engage Fc gamma receptor (FcγR)IIIa/CD16a to stimulate a protective immune response.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about FcγRIIIa function that draws from established scientific knowledge in immunology.

claim: Increasing the FcγRIIIa/IgG1 interaction improves the immune response.
source: Increasing the FcγRIIIa/IgG1 interaction improves the immune response and thus represents a strategy to improve therapeutic efficacy.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is presented as a known fact.

claim: FcγRIIIa is a heavily glycosylated receptor.
source: FcγRIIIa is a heavily glycosylated receptor and glycan composition affects antibody-binding affinity.
evidence: This is a structural characteristic of FcγRIIIa supported by established knowledge.

claim: Glycan composition affects FcγRIIIa antibody-binding affinity.
source: FcγRIIIa is a heavily glycosylated receptor and glycan composition affects antibody-binding affinity.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research from the authors' laboratory and is presented as established knowledge.

claim: Natural killer (NK) cell N-glycan composition affects the potency of antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC).
source: Though our laboratory previously demonstrated that natural killer (NK) cell N-glycan composition affected the potency of one key protective mechanism, antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), it was unclear if this effect was due to FcγRIIIa glycosylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous work from the authors' laboratory, as indicated by the citation to their prior research.

claim: Stepwise affinity increases occur with each glycan truncation step in FcγRIIIa.
source: We observed stepwise affinity increases with each glycan truncation step, with the most severely truncated glycoform displaying the highest affinity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically affinity measurements.

claim: The most severely truncated FcγRIIIa glycoform displays the highest antibody-binding affinity.
source: We observed stepwise affinity increases with each glycan truncation step, with the most severely truncated glycoform displaying the highest affinity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The N162 glycan plays a predominant role in regulating FcγRIIIa antibody-binding affinity.
source: Removing the N162 glycan demonstrated its predominant role in regulating antibody-binding affinity, in contrast to four other FcγRIIIa N-glycans.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different glycoforms and mutations.

claim: NK cells expressing the FcγRIIIa V158 allotype exhibit increased ADCC following kifunensine treatment.
source: NK cells expressing the FcγRIIIa V158 allotype exhibited increased ADCC following kifunensine treatment to limit N-glycan processing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The N162 glycan is required for increased NK cell ADCC following kifunensine treatment.
source: Notably, an increase was not observed with cells expressing the FcγRIIIa V158 S164A variant that lacks N162 glycosylation, indicating that the N162 glycan is required for increased NK cell ADCC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing wildtype and S164A variant NK cells.

claim: FG loop residues proximal to the N162 glycosylation site show large chemical shift perturbations following glycan truncation.
source: FG loop residues proximal to the N162 glycosylation site showed large chemical shift perturbations following glycan truncation.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The composition of the N162 glycan stabilizes the FG loop and thus the antibody-binding site.
source: These data support a model for the regulation of FcγRIIIa affinity and NK cell ADCC whereby composition of the N162 glycan stabilizes the FG loop and thus the antibody-binding site.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the NMR and affinity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NK cells require binding of antibodies to only a single receptor type, FcγRIIIa/CD16a, to elicit ADCC.
source: NK cells require binding of antibodies to only a single receptor type, Fc gamma receptor IIIa (FcγRIIIa/CD16a), to elicit ADCC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: NK cells expressing the higher affinity FcγRIIIa V158 allotype demonstrate greater ADCC than those expressing the weaker-binding F158 allotype.
source: NK cells expressing the higher affinity FcγRIIIa V158 allotype demonstrate greater ADCC than those expressing the weaker-binding F158 allotype (hereafter referred to as V158F) (Bruhns et al., 2009; Hayes et al., 2017; Cartron et al., 2002; Weng and Levy, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Improving the FcγRIIIa-binding affinity of antibodies increases ADCC and therapeutic potency.
source: Furthermore, improving the FcγRIIIa-binding affinity of antibodies, which bind through the Fc region, likewise increases ADCC and therapeutic potency (Presta et al., 2002; Mössner et al., 2010; Townsend et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FcγRIIIa glycosylation affects antibody-binding affinity, with oligomannose-type N-glycans providing higher affinity interactions.
source: We determined that FcγRIIIa glycosylation affected antibody-binding affinity, with oligomannose-type N-glycans providing higher affinity interactions (Patel et al., 2018; Subedi and Barb, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Oligomannose N-glycans are minimally remodeled forms that are not expected at high percentages on secreted proteins.
source: Oligomannose N-glycans are minimally remodeled forms that are not expected at high percentages on secreted proteins in contrast to highly remodeled complex-type glycans found on most serum glycoproteins (Moremen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about glycan processing, supported by a citation.

claim: The N162 glycan is located near the interface formed with the antibody Fc.
source: Among the five FcγRIIIa N-glycosylation sites, the composition of the glycan at N162 is responsible for increased antibody-binding affinity and is located near the interface formed with the antibody Fc (Subedi and Barb, 2018; Sondermann et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: FcγRIIIa purified from NK cells of healthy human donors contains both complex-type and oligomannose glycoforms at the N162 site.
source: Furthermore, we identified a high degree of glycan compositional heterogeneity at the N162 site on FcγRIIIa purified from NK cells of healthy human donors including both complex-type and oligomannose glycoforms (Patel et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2020; Patel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by prior research from the authors' laboratory.

claim: YTS cells express FcγRIIIa with extensive glycan processing, including the N162 site with predominantly hybrid and complex-type glycoforms.
source: YTS cells, a key cytotoxic human NK cell line used for these studies, express FcγRIIIa with extensive glycan processing, including the N162 site with predominantly hybrid and complex-type glycoforms (Patel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by prior research from the authors' laboratory.

claim: High-affinity FcγRIIIa forms are more abundant in adult donors compared to children.
source: The N162 glycan heterogeneity on NK cells is reflected in the presence of both high-affinity and low-affinity FcγRIIIa forms in the periphery of healthy donors, with high-affinity forms more abundant in adult donors compared to children (Benavente et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: NK cells with limited N-glycan remodeling capability demonstrate increased ADCC.
source: NK cells with limited N-glycan remodeling capability, following either treatment with kifunensine or knockdown of the bottleneck glycan processing enzyme MGAT1, demonstrated increased ADCC (Benavente et al., 2024; Rodriguez Benavente et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research from the authors' laboratory.

claim: FcγRIIIa proteins with mutations at the antibody-binding interface reveal a wide range of affinities.
source: The resulting FcγRIIIa proteins revealed a wide range of affinities between those slightly higher than wildtype (S164A) to a handful with no apparent binding at 2.5 µM to fucosylated IgG1 Fc (Y132S, W90A, W113A; Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements presented in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The S164A mutation results in slightly higher affinity than wildtype FcγRIIIa.
source: The resulting FcγRIIIa proteins revealed a wide range of affinities between those slightly higher than wildtype (S164A) to a handful with no apparent binding at 2.5 µM to fucosylated IgG1 Fc (Y132S, W90A, W113A; Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: Y132S, W90A, and W113A FcγRIIIa mutations show no apparent binding at 2.5 µM to fucosylated IgG1 Fc.
source: The resulting FcγRIIIa proteins revealed a wide range of affinities between those slightly higher than wildtype (S164A) to a handful with no apparent binding at 2.5 µM to fucosylated IgG1 Fc (Y132S, W90A, W113A; Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: Two key regions for FcγRIIIa antibody binding center around Y132 and a pair of tryptophan residues (W90 and W113).
source: Mapping the impact of these mutations onto a FcγRIIIa structural model identified two key regions consistent with empirically derived structural models of the antibody:receptor complex (Sondermann et al., 2000), though our data provide greater detail showing how each residue affects affinity. These two regions center around Y132 and a pair of tryptophan residues (W90 and W113), which overlaps with the contact interface identified by X-ray crystallography (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison with prior structural studies.

claim: The K161A mutation reduces FcγRIIIa affinity by tenfold.
source: Surprisingly, although the K161A mutation reduces affinity by tenfold, mutating adjacent residues including S160 showed little direct impact on affinity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: Mutating S160 shows little direct impact on FcγRIIIa affinity.
source: Surprisingly, although the K161A mutation reduces affinity by tenfold, mutating adjacent residues including S160 showed little direct impact on affinity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: F153 and I88 mutations minimally impact FcγRIIIa affinity (less than twofold).
source: It was likewise surprising that the solvent-exposed, large hydrophobic side chains of F153 and I88 minimally impacted affinity (less than twofold).
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: A majority of the FcγRIIIa mutations only impacted affinity by threefold or less.
source: A majority of the mutations only impacted affinity by threefold or less.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: YTS cells expressing the FcγRIIIa S164A variant display the highest average ADCC.
source: Within our library, YTS cells expressing the FcγRIIIa S164A variant displayed the highest average ADCC and the tryptophan mutants showed no detectable ADCC, indicating higher affinity leads to higher ADCC (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: YTS cells expressing FcγRIIIa tryptophan mutants show no detectable ADCC.
source: Within our library, YTS cells expressing the FcγRIIIa S164A variant displayed the highest average ADCC and the tryptophan mutants showed no detectable ADCC, indicating higher affinity leads to higher ADCC (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data.

claim: Higher FcγRIIIa affinity leads to higher ADCC.
source: Within our library, YTS cells expressing the FcγRIIIa S164A variant displayed the highest average ADCC and the tryptophan mutants showed no detectable ADCC, indicating higher affinity leads to higher ADCC (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between affinity and ADCC measurements.

claim: A plot of affinity versus ADCC potency demonstrates a trend linking high affinity and greater ADCC.
source: A plot of the affinity for each variant versus the ADCC potency demonstrated a trend linking high affinity and greater ADCC.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Greater FcγRIIIa antibody-binding affinity on NK cells increases ADCC.
source: These results indicate that greater FcγRIIIa antibody-binding affinity on NK cells increases ADCC and FcγRIIIa engineering represents an unexplored avenue to improve NK cell-mediated immunotherapies.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing correlation between affinity and ADCC.

claim: Antibody fucosylation reduces affinity for FcγRIIIa.
source: Shields et al. previously showed that antibody fucosylation reduces affinity for FcγRIIIa (Shields et al., 2002), and it is known that the N162 glycan mediates the response to fucose, though the underlying mechanism remains disputed (Ferrara et al., 2011; Mizushima et al., 2011; Sakae et al., 2017; Falconer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The N162 glycan mediates the response to antibody fucose.
source: Shields et al. previously showed that antibody fucosylation reduces affinity for FcγRIIIa (Shields et al., 2002), and it is known that the N162 glycan mediates the response to fucose, though the underlying mechanism remains disputed (Ferrara et al., 2011; Mizushima et al., 2011; Sakae et al., 2017; Falconer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: FcγRIIIa variants largely exhibit decreased affinity compared with wildtype when evaluated against fucosylated IgG1 Fc.
source: These variants largely exhibited decreased affinity compared with the wildtype FcγRIIIa when evaluated against fucosylated IgG1 Fc (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Each FcγRIIIa variant displays reduced sensitivity to fucose when the N162 glycan is absent.
source: Surprisingly, each variant displayed reduced sensitivity to fucose when the N162 glycan was absent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements comparing variants with and without the N162 glycan.

claim: The impact of fucose reduces from a 2.2-fold average effect when the N162 glycan is present to a 1.3-fold change when the N162 glycan is absent.
source: The impact of fucose reduced from a 2.2-fold average effect when the N162 glycan was present to a 1.3-fold change when the N162 glycan was absent (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: F153S and R155S FcγRIIIa variants lacking the N162 glycan bind antibody glycoforms with higher affinity than wildtype.
source: The F153S and R155S variants lacking the N162 glycan are notable outliers in that both bind antibody glycoforms with higher affinity than the wildtype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: Intermolecular glycan-glycan contacts provide minimal stability to the antibody/receptor complex.
source: These data also are consistent with the hypothesis that intermolecular glycan-glycan contacts provide minimal stability to the antibody/receptor complex because higher affinity was achieved by removing the N162 glycan.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that removing the N162 glycan increases affinity.

claim: Sequential removal of terminal sugars from FcγRIIIa N-glycans results in a step-wise increase in affinity.
source: We observed a step-wise increase in affinity following the removal of each type of terminal sugar (Figure 2C, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements of glycosidase-treated FcγRIIIa.

claim: Removing the core α-linked mannose or sialic acid residues from FcγRIIIa shows the greatest change for a single removal step.
source: Removing the core α-linked mannose or sialic acid residues showed the greatest change for a single removal step, increasing affinity by fivefold or twofold respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: Overall glycan truncation decreases FcγRIIIa KD by 12-fold.
source: Overall, glycan truncation was observed to decrease KD by 12-fold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: The S164A variant shows only a fourfold overall change in affinity with glycan truncation.
source: While the S164A affinities followed the same trend as the wildtype, the changes were substantially smaller in magnitude with only a fourfold overall change.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: Removing the core α-linked mannose residues from S164A increases affinity by less than 1.5-fold.
source: The removal of the core α-linked mannose residues increased affinity by less than 1.5-fold, in contrast to the fivefold increase observed for the wildtype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: The N162 glycan composition has the primary contribution to antibody-binding affinity.
source: These results demonstrate the primary contribution of the N162 glycan composition to antibody-binding affinity, with smaller contributions from N-glycans at the remaining four sites.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing affinity changes in wildtype versus S164A variant.

claim: N-glycan processing inhibits FcγRIIIa antibody-binding affinity.
source: Furthermore, these data demonstrate the negative impact of adding additional residues throughout the processing pathway, further indicating that N-glycan processing inhibits antibody-binding affinity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glycan truncation increases affinity.

claim: YTS cells expressing wildtype FcγRIIIa demonstrate increased ADCC following kifunensine treatment.
source: As expected based on our lab's previous work, the YTS cells expressing the FcγRIIIa wildtype demonstrated increased ADCC following kifunesine treatment (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data presented in Figure 3.

claim: YTS cells expressing the V158F variant demonstrate a 1.4-fold ADCC increase following kifunensine treatment.
source: Cells expressing the V158F variant likewise demonstrated a 1.4-fold ADCC increase following kifunensine treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data.

claim: YTS cells expressing the T167Y variant show increased ADCC following kifunensine treatment.
source: We observed a similar result for YTS cells expressing the T167Y variant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data.

claim: YTS FcγRIIIa S164A cells demonstrate no increase in ADCC following kifunensine treatment.
source: However, YTS FcγRIIIa cells lacking only the N162 glycan through the S164A mutation demonstrated no increase following kifunensine treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data.

claim: YTS cells expressing wildtype FcγRIIIa evaluated with afucosylated antibody show a significant increase following kifunensine treatment compared to those evaluated with fucosylated antibody.
source: The YTS cells expressing wildtype FcγRIIIa evaluated with afucosylated antibody showed a significant increase following kifunensine treatment compared to those evaluated with the fucosylated antibody (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data presented in Figure 3.

claim: No further benefit is observed for the S164A variant with afucosylated antibodies following kifunensine treatment.
source: Notably, we observed no further benefit for the S164A variant with afucosylated antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data.

claim: The N162 glycan is a critical mediator of increased ADCC responses following inhibiting both NK cell glycan remodeling and antibody fucosylation.
source: This result indicates that the N162 glycan is a critical mediator of increased ADCC responses following inhibiting both NK cell glycan remodeling and antibody fucosylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that S164A does not show increased ADCC with kifunensine or afucosylated antibodies.

claim: N-glycoproteins represent a significant challenge for NMR spectroscopy due to exceptional line broadening and signal loss.
source: N-glycoproteins, including FcγRIIIa, represent a significant challenge for NMR spectroscopy due to exceptional line broadening and thus signal loss resulting from the presence of extended N-glycans that slow molecular tumbling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the technical challenges of NMR spectroscopy of glycoproteins.

claim: N-glycoproteins are seldom investigated by NMR despite their prevalence in the human proteome.
source: As a result of these physical limitations, N-glycoproteins are seldom investigated by NMR despite their prevalence in the human proteome (22% of the human proteome enters the secretory pathway and contains an N-glycosylation site).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by general knowledge.

claim: 22% of the human proteome enters the secretory pathway and contains an N-glycosylation site.
source: As a result of these physical limitations, N-glycoproteins are seldom investigated by NMR despite their prevalence in the human proteome (22% of the human proteome enters the secretory pathway and contains an N-glycosylation site).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the human proteome.

claim: The spectrum of FcγRIIIa N38Q/N74Q/N169Q variant with two N-glycans improved compared to FcγRIIIa with five N-glycans.
source: The spectrum of the FcγRIIIa N38Q/N74Q/N169Q variant with two N-glycans improved and peak positions proved highly comparable to those from FcγRIIIa with five N-glycans.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: Peak positions of FcγRIIIa N38Q/N74Q/N169Q are highly comparable to those from FcγRIIIa with five N-glycans.
source: The spectrum of the FcγRIIIa N38Q/N74Q/N169Q variant with two N-glycans improved and peak positions proved highly comparable to those from FcγRIIIa with five N-glycans.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: 87% of backbone N resonances were assigned in FcγRIIIa N38Q/N74Q/N169Q.
source: As a result, we assigned a high percentage of the backbone resonances (87% N, 90% HN, 86% CO, 86% CA) and almost all the peaks in the 2D HSQC-TROSY spectrum (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data presented in Figure 4.

claim: 90% of backbone HN resonances were assigned in FcγRIIIa N38Q/N74Q/N169Q.
source: As a result, we assigned a high percentage of the backbone resonances (87% N, 90% HN, 86% CO, 86% CA) and almost all the peaks in the 2D HSQC-TROSY spectrum (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: 86% of backbone CO resonances were assigned in FcγRIIIa N38Q/N74Q/N169Q.
source: As a result, we assigned a high percentage of the backbone resonances (87% N, 90% HN, 86% CO, 86% CA) and almost all the peaks in the 2D HSQC-TROSY spectrum (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: 86% of backbone CA resonances were assigned in FcγRIIIa N38Q/N74Q/N169Q.
source: As a result, we assigned a high percentage of the backbone resonances (87% N, 90% HN, 86% CO, 86% CA) and almost all the peaks in the 2D HSQC-TROSY spectrum (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: This is the only NMR resonance assignment of a glycoprotein with two N-glycans attached.
source: To our knowledge, this is the only NMR resonance assignment of a glycoprotein with two N-glycans attached.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the work based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: A small handful of NMR assignments exist for proteins with one N-glycan, notably CD2 and the Fc region of IgG1.
source: A small handful of assignments exist for proteins with one N-glycan, notably CD2 and the Fc region of IgG1 (a thermostable dimer) (Wyss et al., 1995; Yagi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Peak positions between FcγRIIIa and FcγRIIIb show a high degree of overlap but a few notable differences.
source: A comparison of the peak positions between the FcγRIIIa assignment and a previous assignment of the similar FcγRIIIb protein reveals a high degree of overlap but a few notable differences (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data comparing the two proteins.

claim: FcγRIIIa and FcγRIIIb differ by eight amino acids.
source: These two proteins differ by eight amino acids, though FcγRIIIb was expressed in Escherichia coli and thus is not glycosylated (Yogo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the sequence differences between these proteins, supported by a citation.

claim: FcγRIIIb was expressed in Escherichia coli and thus is not glycosylated.
source: These two proteins differ by eight amino acids, though FcγRIIIb was expressed in Escherichia coli and thus is not glycosylated (Yogo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the expression system and its consequences, supported by a citation.

claim: N-glycosylation of N45 and N162 residues reveals minimal impact on the backbone peak positions for these asparagine residues.
source: Surprisingly, the N-glycosylation of the N45 and N162 residues revealed minimal impact on the backbone peak positions for these asparagine residues.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data comparing glycosylated and non-glycosylated forms.

claim: A few residues show evidence for the sampling of multiple conformations, notably V158 and K161.
source: A few residues showed evidence for the sampling of multiple conformations, notably V158 and K161.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data showing multiple peaks for these residues.

claim: V158 and K161 are located on the FG loop that contains the N162 glycan.
source: These residues are located on the FG loop that contains the N162 glycan.
evidence: This is a structural fact about the location of these residues.

claim: V158 shows a single peak with the (1)GlcNAc glycoform.
source: The peaks simplify as the glycan becomes shorter, up to the point of a single peak observed for V158 with the (1)GlcNAc glycoform that may indicate either sampling of a single conformation or more rapid exchange between two or more conformations.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: Chemical shift perturbations map to residues proximal to the five N-glycosylation sites when comparing complex-type to Man5 N-glycans.
source: Mapping the chemical shift perturbations to the primary sequence revealed residues proximal to the five N-glycosylation sites when comparing the receptor with complex-type glycans to that with Man5 N-glycans (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Truncation to the (1)GlcNAc glycoform causes greater changes to the regions around the N45 and N162 glycans.
source: Truncation to the (1)GlcNAc glycoform caused greater changes to the regions around the N45 and N162 glycans (Figure 5D and F).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Features associated with the (1)GlcNAc spectra represent conformations that promote higher affinity interactions.
source: Features associated with the (1)GlcNAc spectra represent conformations that promote higher affinity interactions as this glycoform binds antibody with the greatest affinity of those evaluated.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between NMR data and affinity measurements.

claim: A recent structure isolated one conformation of the FG loop that differed from those previously observed.
source: A recent structure isolated one conformation of the FG loop that differed from those previously observed, mostly through structures bound to IgG1 Fc (Sondermann et al., 2000; Falconer et al., 2018; Kakiuchi-Kiyota et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: In the recent structure of glycosylated FcγRIIIa, the FG loop is free from contacts with the Fc ligand or with the crystal lattice.
source: In this recent structure of glycosylated FcγRIIIa, the FG loop is free from contacts with the Fc ligand or with the crystal lattice, revealing a conformation that is sterically prohibited in the complex with antibody (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from X-ray crystallography.

claim: To bind antibody, the N162 glycan and the FG loop must reorient to avoid steric clashes with IgG1 Fc.
source: To bind, the N162 glycan and the FG loop must reorient to avoid steric clashes with IgG1 Fc.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis comparing bound and unbound conformations.

claim: The backbone conformation of the supporting beta strands shows minimal displacement.
source: The backbone conformation of the supporting beta strands shows minimal displacement, though larger backbone deviations are observed for the L157, K161 and S164 residues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Larger backbone deviations are observed for L157, K161 and S164 residues.
source: The backbone conformation of the supporting beta strands shows minimal displacement, though larger backbone deviations are observed for the L157, K161 and S164 residues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The presence of distinct FG loop conformations is supported by NMR spectra showing two peaks, including V158 and K161.
source: The presence of these distinct conformations is supported by the NMR spectra showing two peaks, including V158 and K161 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: 1 µs all-atom MD simulations found the presence of both FG loop conformations identified by X-ray crystallography in trajectories of FcγRIIIa with complex-type or Man5 N-glycans.
source: We investigated conformational sampling further with 1 µs all-atom MD simulations and found the presence of both conformations identified by X-ray crystallography in trajectories of FcγRIIIa with complex-type or Man5 N-glycans (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: MD simulations initialized with the bound state conformation sampled both conformations throughout the experiment.
source: These simulations were initialized with a starting structure representing the bound state conformation but sampled both conformations throughout the experiment.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Non-covalent interactions form between the aliphatic portion of the R155 sidechain and the hydrophobic surface of the (1)GlcNAc residue in the ligand-bound conformation.
source: One notable detail from these simulations was the formation of non-covalent interactions between the aliphatic portion of the R155 sidechain with the hydrophobic surface of the (1)GlcNAc residue in the ligand-bound conformation that were absent in the unliganded conformation.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The FcγRIIIa R155S (1)GlcNAc glycoform binds IgG1 Fc with a fivefold weaker affinity compared to the wildtype in the same glycoform.
source: The FcγRIIIa R155S (1)GlcNAc glycoform bound IgG1 Fc with a fivefold weaker affinity compared to the wildtype in the same glycoform (Figure 6C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: R155S binding is comparable to the S164A mutant lacking the N162-glycan.
source: The R155S binding is comparable to the S164A mutant lacking the N162-glycan, and mutation of a nearby residue retaining the N-glycan F153S retains the benefit of the (1)GlcNAc/R155 interaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: F153S mutation retains the benefit of the (1)GlcNAc/R155 interaction.
source: The R155S binding is comparable to the S164A mutant lacking the N162-glycan, and mutation of a nearby residue retaining the N-glycan F153S retains the benefit of the (1)GlcNAc/R155 interaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: The R155 sidechain stabilizes the binding-competent conformation.
source: These data demonstrate a role for the R155 sidechain to stabilize the binding-competent conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the affinity measurements and MD simulation data.

claim: The N162 glycan regulates NK cell ADCC.
source: Removing the N162 glycan eliminated the ADCC gains following inhibiting NK cell N-glycan processing with kifunensine, demonstrating a unique role for this protein modification in the immune system.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that S164A does not show increased ADCC with kifunensine.

claim: The N162 glycan composition is variable on endogenous NK cells, likely providing a range of ADCC potency.
source: Thus, the FcγRIIIa N162 glycan composition is variable on endogenous NK cells, likely providing a range of ADCC potency.
evidence: This is inferred from prior observations of N162 glycan heterogeneity.

claim: Affinities lower than 300 nM show little, if any, ADCC.
source: Affinities lower than 300 nM showed little, if any, ADCC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data.

claim: Affinities greater than 300 nM show substantial cytotoxicity with a sharp increase at greater affinities.
source: Affinities greater than 300 nM showed substantial cytotoxicity with a sharp increase at greater affinities indicating that greater FcγRIIIa antibody-binding affinity is expected to further increase ADCC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data.

claim: Greater FcγRIIIa antibody-binding affinity is expected to further increase ADCC.
source: Affinities greater than 300 nM showed substantial cytotoxicity with a sharp increase at greater affinities indicating that greater FcγRIIIa antibody-binding affinity is expected to further increase ADCC.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between affinity and ADCC.

claim: Both the FG loop and its attached N162 glycan move from a position in the unliganded state that allows maximum flexibility to a restricted state to accommodate Fc binding.
source: Both the FG loop and its attached N162 glycan move from a position in the unliganded state that allows maximum flexibility to a restricted state to accommodate Fc binding (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis comparing bound and unbound states.

claim: A conformational entropy penalty is introduced upon complex formation by shifting the N162 glycan to a restricted space between surfaces formed by the Fc and FcγRIIIa polypeptide.
source: We believe this result is best explained by a conformational entropy penalty introduced upon complex formation by shifting the N162 glycan to a restricted space between surfaces formed by the Fc and FcγRIIIa polypeptide.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: A loss of N162 glycan conformational entropy alone is sufficient to explain the observed 1.7–2.2 kcal mol–1 difference in binding affinities.
source: A loss of N162 glycan conformational entropy alone is sufficient to explain the observed 1.7–2.2 kcal mol–1 difference in binding affinities (Subedi and Barb, 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical calculation based on thermodynamic principles and prior data.

claim: The estimated difference between the change of conformational entropy upon binding for complex-type and Man5 N-glycans is 4.8 kcal mol–1.
source: A simple calculation, assuming three equally populated conformations in the unliganded state per rotatable bond, provides an estimate of the difference between the change of conformational entropy upon binding for the complex-type and Man5 N-glycans of 4.8 kcal mol–1 (Imberty et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a theoretical calculation based on assumptions about conformational sampling.

claim: The entropic penalty is likely alleviated by stabilizing interactions between the (1)GlcNAc residue and the R155 sidechain.
source: The entropic penalty is likely also alleviated by stabilizing interactions between the (1)GlcNAc residue and the R155 sidechain, explaining why the truncated glycoform displays a greater affinity than the S164A variant that lacks the N162 glycan.
evidence: This is inferred from the affinity measurements and MD simulation data.

claim: W90 and W113 are conserved among human low-affinity FcγRs.
source: W90 and W113 are conserved among human low-affinity FcγRs and sandwich the IgG1 Fc P329 residue which is likewise conserved in IgG and IgE (Sondermann et al., 2000; Tamm and Schmidt, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sequence conservation, supported by citations.

claim: IgG1 Fc P329 residue is conserved in IgG and IgE.
source: W90 and W113 are conserved among human low-affinity FcγRs and sandwich the IgG1 Fc P329 residue which is likewise conserved in IgG and IgE (Sondermann et al., 2000; Tamm and Schmidt, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sequence conservation, supported by citations.

claim: The proline sandwich interaction is the primary binding interaction in FcγRs.
source: Previous studies suggest that this proline sandwich interaction is the primary binding interaction in FcγRs, which is consistent with results that mutation abolished binding.
evidence: This is supported by prior research and the experimental observation that mutations abolish binding.

claim: YTS cells expressing the FcγRIIIa W90A or W113A mutants do not exhibit measurable ADCC.
source: The importance of W90 and W113 is also supported by our functional data showing YTS cells expressing the FcγRIIIa W90A or W113A mutants do not exhibit measurable ADCC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data.

claim: I88A binds with twofold lower affinity than V158.
source: Within this same region, I88A bound with twofold lower than V158.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: The Y132S mutation eliminates FcγRIIIa binding.
source: The Y132S mutation eliminated binding, likely due to removing numerous stabilizing interactions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: IgG1 Fc D265 residue is critical for FcγRIIIa binding.
source: The IgG1 Fc D265 residue is critical and thought to stabilize the N297 glycan, in which mutation abolishes FcγRIIIa binding (Baudino et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The K120A mutation reduces FcγRIIIa binding by fivefold.
source: We found the K120A mutation reduced binding by fivefold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: Mutations of L157 and S160 do not change FcγRIIIa affinity.
source: While mutation of residues L157 and S160 did not change affinity, K161A lowered affinity by tenfold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental affinity measurements.

claim: K161 is not predicted to make direct contact with Fc.
source: The impact of the K161 mutation is interesting because K161 is not predicted to make direct contact with Fc, although it may contribute to loop stabilization or may transiently contact the IgG1 Fc (Sondermann et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and prior research.

claim: FcγRIIIa engineering through substitutions aimed at stabilizing the Fc-bound conformation in the absence of ligand is expected to promote affinity and ADCC.
source: These results indicate FcγRIIIa engineering through substitutions aimed at stabilizing the Fc-bound conformation in the absence of ligand is expected to promote affinity and ADCC.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Affinity gains are possible beyond that provided by the tighter-binding V158 allotype.
source: Affinity gains are possible beyond that provided by the tighter-binding V158 allotype, and we demonstrate that relatively small affinity improvements have a substantial impact on ADCC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing variants with higher affinity than V158.

claim: Relatively small affinity improvements have a substantial impact on ADCC.
source: Affinity gains are possible beyond that provided by the tighter-binding V158 allotype, and we demonstrate that relatively small affinity improvements have a substantial impact on ADCC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ADCC assay data.
